questions.q: On a stage with no camera to give a close-up, how does a production most often tell the audience whom to watch?
choices: By giving them the most lines
By lighting: the eye goes to the brightest area
questions.explain: Light does the camera's job on stage: a special, a follow spot or a narrowing of light directs focus.

questions.q: An actor keeps drifting toward the back of the stage during a scene partner's big speech, forcing the partner to turn away from the audience. What is this called?
questions.explain: Upstage is the back of the stage; standing upstage of someone forces them to turn their back on the audience.

questions.q: Which designer argued that three-dimensional spaces and light changing like music should replace flat painted scenery?
questions.explain: Appia's Music and the Art of the Theatre (1899) made light the unifying force of a production.

questions.q: Near the end of The Cherry Orchard, a distant sound like a breaking string returns, followed by an axe on the trees. What is the sound doing?
choices: A sound cue that recurs to carry the play's mood and meaning
A Brechtian song that comments on the action
questions.explain: A single recurring sound can hold a play's sense of loss; Chekhov writes it into the stage directions.

questions.q: A playwright wants a scene to end on a sharp, shocking image. Which choice fits best?
choices: A snap blackout right after the image
questions.explain: A blackout is theatre's hard cut; the last image before darkness is what the audience carries forward.

questions.q: A director stages a play on a bare floor with two chairs and has actors mime their props. Whose idea is she drawing on?
questions.explain: Brook argued any empty space can be a stage; Our Town shows the same principle.

questions.q: Why would Brecht leave the stage lights in full view of the audience?
choices: To make the audience aware it's in a theatre, so it thinks rather than drifts into mood
questions.explain: Visible machinery was one of Brecht's ways of making the familiar strange.

ideas: Because a live audience can look anywhere, light has to do the camera's job of choosing where the eye goes.
Light should shape three-dimensional space and change like music, rather than illuminate painted scenery.
Any empty space can be a stage: a person crossing it while someone watches is enough for theatre.
Where actors stand, near or far, high or low, facing out or turned away, makes a picture that tells the audience who matters.
